before: @property decorates the getter function so duration.minutes calls that getter through attribute syntax; callers do not write duration.minutes(). The getter returns the current stored value. A leading underscore in _minutes marks an internal convention, not enforced security.

@minutes.setter adds a setter to that same named property. Assignment duration.minutes = value invokes the setter with the receiver and new value. Here it checks the value before storing it in _minutes. Raising ValueError rejects a negative value without changing the old state; a property setter does not supply an assignment return value to the caller.

The getter reads self._minutes, not self.minutes. Reading self.minutes inside its own getter would re-enter the property recursively. The setter similarly stores the backing attribute instead of assigning the managed name again.

after:
A getter is a method that supplies a value when you read a property. With `@property`, reading `duration.minutes` calls the getter. You leave off `()`.

The getter reads the saved `_minutes`. Its leading underscore is a hint that this is internal data. Python does not make it private.

A setter is a method that handles a new property value. `@minutes.setter` adds one for `minutes`.

Assigning `duration.minutes = value` calls it with the object and the new value. It checks before saving to `_minutes`. A negative value raises `ValueError`, so the old minutes stay unchanged.

The assignment does not give back the setter's return value.

The getter reads self._minutes, not self.minutes. Reading self.minutes inside the getter would call the getter again and again. The setter also stores the value in self._minutes instead of assigning to the managed name again.

Complete the property. Accept the exercise's zero and positive numbers. Reject negative starting values and updates with `ValueError` before changing the saved minutes.

Leave the supplied helpers unchanged. They try known negative inputs, and `__rejects_negative` checks that the old minutes remain. They do not test every possible input.

For extra practice, give another property its own value check. Try one allowed update and one rejected update.
